record.tranche_reason: The study constructs a harmful-minus-harmless mean-activation refusal direction and applies it to residual activations, then measures safety and benign performance as steering is withdrawn. Its intervention is a single selected steering layer, not the claim’s all-layer, all-position ablation.
record.gate_note: The study reports results for steering duration, safety after steering withdrawal, and benign performance. Prediction C-indices and feature ablations assess the withdrawal predictor, not refusal itself, so they are not rows. Results about cited work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study's main goal is a withdrawal schedule, so the withdrawn-versus-maintained rows are method evaluations. It also reports unsteered versus persistent-steering results (Table 1) for an Arditi-style harmful-minus-harmless direction added at one layer. Those bear on V1's 'adding it induces refusal' part, in a new setting: jailbreak prompts, benign over-refusal benchmarks, and Qwen3 models.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that refusal steering can end early, predicted per prompt from the first two tokens' refusal projection. Safety stays close to persistent steering while exposure, over-refusal and capability loss fall. Withdrawal boundaries depend on model, strength, decoding and evaluator.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the harmful-minus-benign mean-activation refusal direction and residual-stream addition, but applies it at a selected steering layer and studies finite schedules and adaptive withdrawal rather than ablation at every layer and position.
record.method_sensitivity: Restoration width and withdrawal safety vary with model, safety evaluator, generation length, decoding procedure, steering strength, and steering start time.

fits_no_version.finding: Refusal steering that starts at the first output token reaches safety comparable to persistent steering after a finite window (32–64 tokens at alpha=1). The window shrinks with stronger steering and varies by model and judge.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-direction steering is needed only for an early, model-specific window of output tokens to maintain safety.

fits_no_version.finding: Refusal-then-comply prompts trigger adaptive withdrawal on 318 of 320 attacks but create new safety failures in only 14 (4.4%); Llama accounts for 11.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Triggering early withdrawal of refusal steering rarely bypasses refusal.

record.code_released: An anonymised supplementary notebook is reported; URL not stated.
record.peer_reviewed: Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2027
record.problems: The study tests steering at a selected layer, not all-layer/all-position ablation. Safety conclusions depend on evaluator and generation setting; several post-withdrawal comparisons fail the stated criterion, and some sampled long-generation comparisons have limited continuation coverage. The primary evaluation uses four models.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: Directional ablation (projection out of all layers and positions) removing refusal. Capability retention under ablation. Steering is addition at one selected layer only.
No test of jailbreaks suppressing the direction, or of adversarial training against ablation. The adaptive attack targets the withdrawal rule.
No comparison with multi-direction or cone accounts.
Harmfulness and refusal are not separated.
The direction itself is not transferred across languages, model variants or base-to-instruct. Predictor transfer across models is not direction transfer.
Qwen3 is used, but thinking mode and reasoning are not studied.

missing.what: Unsteered vs persistent-steering HarmBench safety on ID held-out, ISC, GCG, PAIR and StrongREJECT for each model (the direction-addition effect)
Unsteered vs persistent-steering OR-Bench and XSTest answer rates (induced over-refusal on harmless prompts) and MMLU accuracy
Safety by steering start time and strength vs unsteered (start-0 cells vs later starts; alpha 1–3)

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked every withdrawal row to V1. These rows compare the study's own method with persistent steering; both arms are steered, so they cannot test whether the direction mediates refusal. The V1 evidence is the unsteered-vs-persistent contrast in Table 1, which no row captures. Safety is measured as HarmBench non-compliance, not explicit refusal. Steering is addition at a single layer scaled by the projection SD, not the original's procedure. Qwen3 thinking mode is not stated.

versions.untested_parts: Does not project the direction out of every layer and position; does not test whether that full ablation removes refusal; does not test adding the direction to harmless prompts for induced refusals. Steering is applied at one selected layer.
Does not test attacks that suppress the refusal direction or training against its ablation.
Does not compare one refusal direction with an affine, cone, or multiple-direction account.
Does not separate harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
Does not test transfer of the refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base-to-instruct stages.
Does not vary refusal training or measure effects of its timing.
Does not test reasoning models as a category.

relationships.condition: Adding the direction at one layer, alpha=1, greedy decoding, HarmBench judge, held-out jailbreak prompts and benign over-refusal benchmarks, four models
relationships.reason: Based on text, Table 1; no rows link here. Persistent steering raises ID safety over unsteered for all four models (Gemma 75.9→99.8, Qwen3-4B 79.5→95.5, Qwen3-8B 78.5→93.6). It also lowers XSTest answer rates, i.e. induces refusal on harmless prompts (Gemma 80.4→61.2, Qwen3-8B 94.8→70.7).
relationships.display_finding: Persistent addition improved safety across all four models, including Gemma from 75.9 to 99.8, Qwen3-4B from 79.5 to 95.5 and Qwen3-8B from 78.5 to 93.6, while XSTest answer rates fell from 80.4 to 61.2 for Gemma and from 94.8 to 70.7 for Qwen3-8B.

relationships.condition: Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B at alpha=1, and steering started after the first output token
relationships.reason: Based on text (Table 1, Fig. 4). Induction is incomplete: Llama ID safety only 84.0→90.4. Later start times recover much less safety, e.g. Llama start 4, width 64 reaches 71%. Persistent steering also costs MMLU (Llama 39.8→29.8, Qwen3-8B 71.3→52.1).
relationships.display_finding: Llama safety rose from 84.0% to 90.4% but reached only 71% when starting at token four with width 64; persistent steering reduced MMLU from 39.8 to 29.8 for Llama and 71.3 to 52.1 for Qwen3-8B.
